metadata.note: The Raleigh and Gaston Railroad (Raleigh - Gaston 1840, Weldon extension 1853, Louisburg Branch), the Petersburg Railroad's 1838-39 lease operation of its first miles, and the line's Seaboard Air Line (1900-1967), Seaboard Coast Line (1967-1968/1971) and Amtrak (1971-1986) successors as far as the ex-R&G track runs (Raleigh - Norlina - Weldon). Drawn from research/branches/raleigh_and_gaston_railroad.txt in the site repo (DanielMConnolly/historical-trains), researched 2026-11-05. Only the report's main drawable spans are drawn (not its 'strict alternatives'). Before this layer the map drew no part of this railroad and no SAL line between Weldon/Richmond and Raleigh. Features split per drawable span x operator (Rule 4); features of different operators over the same track share identical geometry. State of North Carolina ownership 1845-1851 is treated as the same operator (trains still run as 'the Raleigh and Gaston rail road'); the 1881-1900 'Seaboard Air Line' system name was marketing - the R&G ran its own trains until the 1900 consolidation.

not_yet_sourced: Louisburg Branch: BOTH ends [OPEN] - 1891 is the earliest and 1897 the last CONFIRMED passenger year. 1885-1890 (from the lease) and 1898-1900 unproven; SAL-era passenger end unknown (freight and express only by the Feb 1952 Official Guide). NC Corporation Commission reports 1910-33 and Louisburg's Franklin Times would settle it - and an SAL-era Louisburg feature.

1841-1846 on Raleigh - Gaston: drawn on bracketing passenger evidence (1840, 1847, 1849, 1851) and operation evidence only; a Sept 1843 Standard item about a stage line carrying the mail between Sledge's and Weldon is unread (OCR) and may mean reduced service.
South Gaston - Weldon in 1865: mail contract Aug 1865 but no 1865 passenger evidence; postwar restart drawn 1866 (inclusive years make this invisible on the slider).
Weldon extension opening: 1853 (carolana) vs 1852 (1891 Commission, Wikipedia); 1853 drawn.
Gaston bridge stub after 1853: whether passenger trains still crossed to the north bank 1853-1865 is unknown; drawn only to 1853.

Length of the Gaston stub: the report's '~1 mi' is unsourced; the trace (to OHM's R&G / Greensville & Roanoke junction) is 3.9 mi, consistent with carolana's Gaston - Henderson 42.5 mi. The 1840 Gaston depot site itself is not pinned by any source.
1900 SAL takeover month not verified (carolana: 10 Apr 1900).
SCL 1967-1971 Raleigh - Norlina: routing via Norlina inferred from mileage/running time in the 1969 and March 1971 Silver Star schedules; no SCL timetable printing Henderson or Norlina was read.
Amtrak 1971 start: not checked against a 1971 Amtrak timetable printing Norlina/Henderson. End-day conflict 25 Oct (Wikipedia, Norlina Subdivision) vs 26 Oct 1986 (report).
All headways except 1838 'daily' and 1891's two trains each way are estimates; all speeds are estimates.

segments.note: The Raleigh and Gaston's line worked by the Petersburg Railroad as lessee, which furnished all rolling stock and engines (carolana), from the north-bank Gaston junction with the Greensville & Roanoke; cars ran through to Petersburg. Opened in stages in 1838: Littleton May, Macon June, Ridgeway July, Henderson September (carolana). Passenger cars ran 'to and from Petersburg daily' as far as Littleton by early June 1838 (Richmond Enquirer 5 Jun 1838); in Nov 1838 half the tolls on the operating part were from passengers (Watchman of the South 20 Dec 1838). The extent of 1838 passenger trains beyond Littleton is inferred from carolana's dated openings plus the passenger tolls - no source names Henderson as a passenger point in 1838. Lease ended 1 Dec 1839 when the R&G began to work its own road (carolana); the Henderson - Franklinton extension reached in Nov 1839 is not drawn as Petersburg RR (at most weeks, unproven for passengers). Headway 1440 = one daily round trip, an estimate from 'daily'.
sources: Segment-level: start 1838 from the Richmond Enquirer (5 Jun 1838, trains to Littleton) and carolana's dated openings to Henderson (Sept 1838) with the Watchman of the South's Nov 1838 passenger tolls; end 1839 at the lease's end (carolana). headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, NOT sourced.

segments.note: Raleigh and Gaston's own trains from 1 Dec 1839 (lease to the Petersburg RR ended, carolana); the road reached Raleigh 21 Mar 1840 ('the passenger cars are expected here', North-Carolina Standard 25 Mar 1840), so drawn from 1840. Ran to the north-bank Gaston junction with the Greensville & Roanoke (Petersburg RR) via the 1,040-ft Roanoke River bridge. Positive passenger years: 1840, 1847 (Staunton in an 1847 guide, Fowler), 1849 (hacks meet passengers at Henderson and Warrenton depot, Standard 15 Aug 1849), 1851 (1851 Dinsmore; Petersburg Intelligencer). 1841-1846 rest on OPERATION evidence only (road earning income 1843-46, Standard 1846; sold Dec 1845 as a going road with engines and cars, NY Herald) - no source says passenger service stopped, but none names passengers in those years either; the strict alternative would be 1840 + 1847-1853. State of North Carolina owned it after the 1845 foreclosure until the 11 Sep 1851 reorganization, still run as 'the Raleigh and Gaston rail road' - treated as the same operator, not split. Ends 1853 when the Weldon extension opened (carolana; 1852 per the 1891 Commission and Wikipedia); nothing confirms passenger use of the Gaston bridge stub after that (bridge burned April 1865, never rebuilt). Headway 1440 = one daily train each way, an estimate.

segments.note: Weldon extension opened 1853 (carolana's explicit correction; '1852' in the 1891 NC Railroad Commission report and Wikipedia - conflict, the later year drawn): the extension left the original line at South Gaston (later Thelma) and ran down the south bank to Weldon, meeting the Petersburg RR, the Seaboard & Roanoke and the Wilmington & Weldon. Civil War: ran throughout - 13,033 passengers Jan-May 1861, 104,149 in the year to 31 May 1862 (CSA); passenger receipts of $621,505.94 in the year to 31 May 1865 (15th annual report). April 1865: Gaston and Cedar Creek bridges burned by Confederate order. Raleigh - South Gaston had R&G passenger trains again by August 1865 (Western Democrat ad), so that part is continuous through 1865. The South Gaston - Weldon end has only a mail contract in Aug 1865 (Alexandria Gazette), not passenger evidence; this segment ends at 1865 on the 1864-65 passenger receipts. Headway 1440 = one daily train each way, an estimate.

segments.note: Postwar: first passenger evidence for the whole line to Weldon is 1866 (the re-privatized company advertised the 'Inland Air Line Route' from 1866, carolana; Seaboard & Roanoke trains 'connecting daily at Weldon' from Feb/Apr 1866). 1875 Official Guide lists Weldon, Littleton, Macon, Warrenton, Ridgeway, Henderson, Kittrell's, Franklinton, Wake, Neuse and Mill Brook (Fowler). R&G timetable effective 14 Jun 1891: a 'Pass daily' and a 'Pass mail daily' each way Raleigh - Weldon (State Chronicle) - two trains each way, headway 720 that year; 1440 (one train) is the conservative estimate for earlier decades and is what is recorded here. From 1881 the R&G, Seaboard & Roanoke and Raleigh & Augusta Air Line were marketed as the 'Seaboard Air Line' system under John M. Robinson, but the R&G kept its corporate identity and ran its own trains (1891 Commission lists the R&G's own 'Property Operated'): a marketing alliance, not a change of operator. Ends 1900 at consolidation into the Seaboard Air Line Railway (month not verified; carolana gives 10 Apr 1900 for the SAL's takeover); service continued under the SAL.
sources: Segment-level: start 1866 from carolana (Inland Air Line Route) and the Seaboard & Roanoke report's 1866 Weldon connection; 1875 from Fowler's Official Guide letters; 1891 from the State Chronicle timetable; end 1900 at the SAL consolidation (carolana). headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates except the 1891 two trains each way.

segments.note: Louisburg Railroad (built 1884-85, owner retained its name), leased to and worked by the Raleigh and Gaston as a branch from completion in 1885 (carolana; the 1891 NC Railroad Commission lists it as R&G 'Property Operated'). START IS [OPEN]: 1891 is the earliest CONFIRMED passenger year (the R&G's own timetable of 14 Jun 1891 prints a Louisburg Railroad train each way, State Chronicle) - 1885-1890 passenger service is probable but unproven. END IS [OPEN]: 1897 is the last CONFIRMED year (Gold Leaf 29 Apr 1897: the regular Louisburg train, plus a special run Louisburg - Franklinton for a minstrel troupe), NOT a known end - no source dates when R&G-era service stopped; it likely ran to the 1900 SAL consolidation and on under the SAL, whose passenger end is also unknown (only 'Freight and Express Service only' by the Feb 1952 Official Guide). Do not extend either end without evidence. One round trip timed to main-line trains at Franklinton in 1891 (probably mixed; not stated) - headway 1440.

segments.note: Seaboard Air Line Railway from the 1900 consolidation (month not verified; carolana gives 10 Apr 1900). With the 1900 Norlina - Petersburg - Richmond line open, the ex-Raleigh & Gaston between Norlina and Raleigh became part of the SAL Richmond - Hamlet main line: Silver Meteor, Silver Star, Silver Comet, Sunland and locals. segments.note: Seaboard Coast Line from the 1 Jul 1967 ACL + SAL merger to Amtrak's takeover on 1 May 1971. Confirmed by two published schedules: the 1969 SCL Silver Star (No. 21) Richmond Broad St 4:15 PM - Petersburg 4:53 - Raleigh 7:10 PM (american-rails), and the April 1971 Official Guide (SCL schedules of March 1971) Silver Star Petersburg - Raleigh at mile 502.0 (streamlinerschedules), the same mileage as the SAL's 1947 Silver Comet via Henderson (Raleigh 500.3). Neither prints Norlina or Henderson, so the route via Norlina is inferred: Petersburg - Raleigh in 2 h 17 min and Raleigh at the SAL mileage fit only the ex-SAL line through Norlina (the alternative via Weldon and Selma is ~50 mi longer); the Silver Star kept this route until Oct 1986 (Wikipedia). The Silver Comet also ran this way until 1969. Headway 480 (two to three trains each way) is an ESTIMATE.

Headway 720 matches the Portsmouth Subdivision feature's estimate (two trains each way read off fragmentary 1951 OCR; one in the Tidewater years) - ESTIMATE.
